entries.modern_form: PIE *mer- 'to rub away, wear out, harm' (Pokorny 5. mer-, mera-, pp. 735-737, with the extensions mer-d- and mer-k-) and PIE *mer- 'to die' (Pokorny 4. mer-, p. 735), with the derivatives *mr-to- 'dead', *mor-to- / *mor-t-yo- 'mortal, man'; extended *smerd- 'pain, to bite, to stink' (Pokorny 969-970)
entries.note: Every element of the root box is a real reconstruction and the page numbers are right. Pokorny prints two adjacent lemmas on p.735: '4. mer-, mera-: to die' (with the note '= mer-5 become faded') and '5. mer-, mera-: to rub, wipe; to pack, rob' (pp. 735-737), and ends the second with 'See also: identical with mer-4' - i.e. Pokorny himself unites the two senses exactly as Nourai's box does. Walde-Pokorny II 276 says it explicitly: ‚mer- „sterben“ gilt mit Recht als ein fruehzeitig selbstaendig gewordener Bedeutungsableger von mer „aufreiben“‘ (WLD_Bd2_pages.txt, page header '276 mer-'). Mer-d and Mer-k are Pokorny's extensions inside mer-5 (pp.736-737): mer-d- with Av. morandat, Lat. mordeo, and mer-k- with Av. mahrka- 'death', maraxsh- 'ruin', maranca(i)ti 'destroys'. Mor-to 'mortal man' is Pokorny's 'mor-to- ‚perishable‘ in Old Indic marta-, Avestan masha- ... derived *mor-t/o- in Old Indic martya-, Avestan mashya-, Old Persian martiya-' (p.735). Smerd is Pokorny 970 'smerd-, smord-: to stink', which Pokorny derives from '(s)merd- in Modern High German schmerzen, Latin mordere, s. mer-, merd ‚chafe‘ (above S. 736 f.)'; Watkins/AHD glosses it 'smerd-. Pain. Extension of mer-2', which is Nourai's 'painful' word for word. The AHD numbering 'Mer 2' also follows Watkins ('mer-2, To rub away, harm'), not Pokorny's, and that is what Nourai cites. The only caveat is bibliographic: AHD:1529 is a page of the 1975/76 New College appendix, which is not open online; the same entry in the 1985 standalone Watkins edition is verified below.
entries.note_fa: جعبهٔ ریشه درست است. پوکورنی در صفحهٔ ۷۳۵ دو مدخل پشت سر هم دارد: mer-4 «مردن» و mer-5 «ساییدن، فرسودن» (۷۳۵–۷۳۷) و خود او در پایان مدخل دوم می‌نویسد «همان mer-4 است»؛ والده–پوکورنی (جلد ۲، ص ۲۷۶) روشن‌تر می‌گوید که «مردن» شاخهٔ معنایی مستقل‌شدهٔ «فرسودن» است. Mer-d و Mer-k همان گسترش‌های پوکورنی در صفحات ۷۳۶–۷۳۷ اند (اوستایی morandat و mahrka-، marancaıti) و Smerd همان smerd- صفحهٔ ۹۷۰ است که واتکینز آن را «درد، گسترشِ mer-2» معنی کرده است. پس ادعای نورایی درست است؛ تنها ارجاع AHD:1529 به پیوست چاپ ۱۹۷۵ است که به صورت آزاد در دسترس نیست و همان مدخل از چاپ ۱۹۸۵ واتکینز راستی آزموده شد.

nodes.words: mar 2; mahrka, marathyu; mareta, masa; mardta; gayo-mereta; a-mereta, amasa
nodes.derivation: All six items are genuine Avestan material from *mer-: (a) mar- 'to die' (Bartholomae col. 1143 'mar- V. ‚sterben‘. Praes. mirya-, mariya-; Aor. mari-; PPfP. marata-'), pres. mid. miryeite, with the compounds ava.miryeite and framiryeite; (b) mahrka- 'death' and marathyu- (marathyu-) 'death' - mahrka- belongs to the k-extension (Bartholomae col. 1145 'mark- V. ‚toeten, zerstoeren“ ... Inf. mahrkai, mahrkathai'), i.e. PIE *mer-k-, while maratyu- is *mr-tyu- (Skt. mrtyu-); (c) marata- and mashya- 'mortal man' = PIE *mor-to- and *mor-t-yo-, with the regular Avestan development of *-rt- to -sh- in mashya- (whence also masha-); (d) gayo.marata(n)- 'mortal life' (gaya- 'life' + marata-), the mythical first man, and (e) a-marata- / amasha- 'immortal' with the privative *n-, the epithet of the Amasha Spantas. The one soft spot is 'mardta : everyone': that is Nourai's spelling of the same marata-, and the gloss 'everyone' is not Avestan at all - it comes from Gharib's Sogdian entry 5467 'mrt mrt (mart mart) <Av. marata: everyone, each' (SOD p.218), where 'everyone' translates the Sogdian reduplication, not the Avestan word. So the item is a doublet of 'mareta' with a borrowed gloss.
nodes.derivation_fa: همهٔ صورت‌های این جعبه اوستایی اند و از ریشهٔ *mer-: ستاک mar- «مردن» (بارتولومه، ستون ۱۱۴۳)، mahrka- «مرگ» که به گسترشِ کافی ریشه (*mer-k-) می‌رسد، marathyu- هم‌ریشه با سنسکریت mrtyu-، marata- و mashya- «مردنی، انسان» (در mashya- خوشهٔ *-rt- به -sh- بدل شده)، gayō.marata(n)- «زندگیِ میرا» و a-marata-/amasha- «بی‌مرگ» با پیشوند نفی. تنها ایراد آن است که «mardta: everyone» دوگانهٔ همین marata- است و معنای «همه‌کس» از مدخل سغدیِ غریب (mrt mrt، شمارهٔ ۵۴۶۷، ص ۲۱۸) آمده که ترجمهٔ تکرار سغدی است نه معنای واژهٔ اوستایی. در کل، ادعا با احتیاط پذیرفتنی است.

nodes.words: mordan «مردن ( مرگ )»; mard «مرد ( مردم )»; Kîumars «کیومرث»; amordâd «امرداد ( مرداد )»
nodes.derivation: Every word descends from the Old Iranian material of node #1. (a) mordan < MP murdan / pres. mir- (MacKenzie p.57 'murdan, mir- [YMYTWN-tn'] to die') < OIr. *mar- (Av. mar-, OP a-mariyata), with *mr-ta- giving MP murd, NP mord-; the verbal noun marg 'death' continues Av. mahrka- through MP marg (Horn no. 977 'merg ‚Tod‘: aw. mahrka- ‚Tod‘; phlv. marg'). (b) mard < MP mard (Book Pahlavi mlt', GBRA) < OP martiya- < PIr. *mrtah 'dead, mortal'; the plural-derived mardom < MP mardom (< *martuxma-, 'seed of man') means 'people'. (c) Kiyumars/Gayomard < MP Gayomart < Av. gayo.maratan- 'mortal life', the first man; the Arabised spelling with -th is late (Borhan itself notes the Persian original had no th). (d) amordad/mordad < MP Amurdad < Av. amaratat- 'immortality' (the abstract of a-marata-), the sixth Amahraspand and the fifth month; the popular form mordad is a haplology that reverses the sense, which is why purists write amordad. All four are the standard modern account.

nodes.derivation: The forms are real Middle Persian, taken verbatim from Gharib p.219, but the gloss 'mortal man' is not theirs. Gharib's entry for Sogdian martin(a) 'Eve, Mashiyane' cites 'Khwar. mordan-, MP murdyanag; Pahl. masyanag' - i.e. Murdiyanag/Masyanag is the FEMALE of the pair, Zoroastrian mythology's first woman, while the male is Masya/Masi. Both continue Av. mashya- 'mortal, man' (node #1) with the Middle Persian suffix -anag: *mashya-anaka- > Masyanag. Nyberg (Glossary p.129) sets out the variants and states that 'the forms Khwar. Mard (‚Man‘) and MPrs fem. Murdiyanag are clearly WIr' - i.e. murdiyanag is the genuine south-western Iranian form beside the east-Iranian-looking mashyanag with -sh- for *-rt-. 'Masa : Adam' is the short form Masi/Masya; 'masyoi : Eve' is the Bundahishn variant Masyoi (Mo'in gives it in Latin script at Borhan p.2017). So: right forms, right root, wrong gloss and a female name presented as 'mortal man'.

nodes.derivation: The New Persian forms Mashya and Mashyaneh are the learned continuations of the Pahlavi pair of node #3: MP Masya/Masi 'the first man' > NP mashya, and MP Masyanag/Masyoi > NP mashyaneh (the -ag suffix regularly gives -a/-eh in New Persian: MP -anag > NP -aneh, as in payg > peyk, xanag > xaneh), with the variant mashyo'i taken straight from the Bundahishn. They are not inherited everyday words but names transmitted through the Zoroastrian tradition and the Persian rendering of the Pahlavi books, which is why Borhan-e Qate' and Mo'in discuss them under masya. The arrow Pahlavi to Persian is therefore correct.
nodes.derivation_fa: «مشیا» و «مشیانه» صورت فارسی همان جفت پهلوی Māshyā/Māshyānag اند؛ پسوند -ag فارسی میانه به قاعده در فارسی نو به -ه بدل می‌شود (مانند xānag > خانه)، و صورت «مشیوئی» راست از بندهشن گرفته شده است. این دو واژه میراثی عامیانه نیستند بلکه از راه سنت زردشتی و متن‌های پهلوی به فارسی رسیده اند؛ به همین سبب برهان قاطع و حاشیهٔ معین آن‌ها را ذیل «مشیا» آورده اند. ادعای نورایی درست است.

nodes.derivation: Neither aiwish-mar- nor *vizmar- is an attested Avestan compound; both are reconstructions invented to explain NP pazmurdan, and modern Iranian etymology has abandoned them. Horn (Grundriss no.313, p.69) proposed 'ap. patis bezw. aw. aiwis + mar-' for pizmurden, and that is Nourai's 'awis-mar'. Huebschmann's Persische Studien p.41 - the reference Nourai's own NOTE flags - answers: 'Die von Noeldeke und Horn erwaehnte Form guzs-murdan des Judenpersischen zeigt, dass pizmurdan ‚verwelken‘ ueber aelteres bizmurdan auf *vizmurdan zurueckgeht. Damit faellt Horn's Etymologie, insbesondere piz- aus patis' - hence Nourai's second form 'wizmar'. Cheung's Etymological Dictionary of the Iranian Verb (2007, s.v. *mar 'to die', pp.265-266) settles it differently again: the prefix is *pari-, cf. Choresmian prmy- 'to wither, fade (of plants, fire)', Shughni (Baj.) parmir-/parmud, Wakhi parmor-/parmord- 'to wither', Yidgha parmorya 'withering', all beside NP pazmurdan/pazmir-. Avestan itself compounds mar- only with *ava- and *fra- (Cheung's Liste 43). So the parent box as drawn is not Avestan fact, and its prefix is wrong on the current view.

nodes.derivation: The word is real and old (Shahnameh pazmuraned, Vis o Ramin pizmeridan) and it does belong to this root: it is a prefixed compound of the same verb as mordan, so the arrow to the Mer root is right. What is wrong is the prefix in the parent box. On the modern account (Cheung 2007) NP pazmurdan/pazmir- 'to wither, fade' goes back to *pari-mar-, the same formation as Choresmian prmy-, Shughni parmir-, Wakhi parmor- 'to wither'; *pari- gives Persian paz-/paj- exactly as in pazhuhidan and pazman, the two other words Huebschmann and Mo'in cite in the same breath. Huebschmann had already rejected Horn's patis-/aiwis- in favour of *viz-, and Mo'in's footnote to the Borhan entry repeats Horn's version with the caveat that 'paz is apparently an old error for baz'. Semantically the shift is 'to die (of a plant)' > 'to wilt, fade', the same shift Avestan shows in fra-mar- 'to die, wither'.

nodes.derivation: This box is Pokorny's mer-d- and mer-k- extensions, quoted accurately. Av. 3sg. morandat (= *mrnd-) 'destroys' belongs to mer-d-, beside Skt. mrdnati/mardati 'grinds, crushes' and Lat. mordeo 'I bite'; Av. maranca(i)ti 'injures, destroys' and the s-aorist maraxsh- 'ruin, destruction' belong to mer-k-, beside Skt. marcayati 'injures' and marka- 'death' = Av. mahrka-. Bartholomae sets the whole family under one verb: 'mark- V. ‚toeten, zerstoeren“, und zwar vom Toeten und Zerstoeren ahurischer Schoepfungen. Praes. maranu-, maranca-, ... s-Aor. maraxsh-: mraxsh-; Inf. maranciyai, mahrkai' (col.1145-1146). Kent p.203 gives the d-form under Old Persian: 'mard- vb. ‚crush‘: Av. marad- ‚destroy‘, Skt. mrd- ‚rub, crush‘, Lt. mordet ‚bites‘, pIE *merd-', which is Nourai's 'mared : destroy'. The semantics ('rub away' > 'crush' > 'destroy') is exactly the bridge Walde-Pokorny uses to unite the two mer- roots.

nodes.derivation: All three are Achaemenid Old Persian, and Kent's Lexicon gives them on precisely the pages cited. mar- 'die' is attested in the middle imperfect a-mariyata 'he died' (Bisitun I 43, of Cambyses), with the -ya- present *mr-ya- (Kent's 'mariya'); marta- is the perfect passive participle *mr-to- 'dead'; martiya- 'man, mortal man' is the *mor-t-yo- formation and the ordinary Achaemenid word for 'man' (DB I 21 and dozens more), the direct ancestor of NP mard. Old Persian therefore shows the same three grades as Avestan (full grade in the root, zero grade in the participle, o-grade in the noun) and the arrow root to Old Persian is correct.

nodes.derivation: The Sogdian word is right and the etymology in Gharib's dictionary is the one Nourai copied: '5474 mrty | marti/i ... <OP martiya-, Yaghn. morti' (p.218), with the parallel entry '5455 mrt'y | marti (c)OP martiya | man'. The one correction a modern Iranist would make is the direction of the arrow: Sogdian is an East Iranian language and cannot descend from Old Persian, a South-West Iranian dialect. Sogdian mrty /marti/ 'man' continues Proto-Iranian *mrtya- directly (whence also the Sogdian compound mrtxmy 'man, person' < *mrtaxmaka-, and Yaghnobi morti), so it is a COGNATE of Old Persian martiya-, not a derivative of it. Gharib's '(c)OP martiya-' sign is a comparison mark, and Nourai has turned it into descent.

nodes.derivation: Half of this box is solid and half is Kent's guess. OP mard- 'to crush' is a real verbal root (Kent p.203: 'mard- vb. ‚crush‘: Av. marad- ‚destroy‘, Skt. mrd- ‚rub, crush‘, Lt. mordet ‚bites‘, pIE *merd- (Foy, KZ 35.48)'), and it is the d-extension of *mer- 'to rub away' - so the arrow from the root is right. 'mard-una : crusher of grapes into wine, wine merchant' is not an attested Old Persian word: it is Kent's tentative back-formation from the personal name Marduniya- (Greek Mardonios, the Mardonius of Herodotus, son of Gobryas), which Kent explains as 'perhaps deriv. to *marduna- ‚vintner‘ ... which possibly contains root mard- ‚crush (the grapes in the wine-making)‘', adding 'otherwise Justi, INB 195'. In his morphology he lists the name among 'names denoting occupations, as perhaps in the adjectival derivative, possibly patronymic, Mardun-iya- ‚Vintner's son‘'. So the form should carry an asterisk and the two 'perhaps'es Kent gives it.

nodes.derivation: The word is real - mol/mul 'wine', a literary archaism of the classical poets, and Nourai quotes Onsori for it - but its modern etymology is not this root. Wiktionary, following the standard Iranist account, has: 'Borrowed from Sogdian mwd /mud/ or less likely from Bactrian molo ‚wine‘, both from Proto-Iranian *madu, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *madhu, from Proto-Indo-European *medhu. Doublet of mey.' That is, mol belongs with mey, mead, Sanskrit madhu - the root Nourai himself cross-references in the chart's NOTE ('For another possible root of Persian mol: wine see root Medhu'). The reason the word appears here at all is Kent's parenthesis under Marduniya-: 'perhaps deriv. to *marduna- ‚vintner‘ ... cf. NPers mul ‚wine‘', which was already a guess in 1950 and would in any case require an unexplained loss of the -d-. So the node is a legitimate reference to Kent but is superseded: the modern view puts mol under Medhu.

nodes.derivation: Greek marainein 'to waste away, wither, quench' is a certain member of this root: Pokorny puts it in mer-5 ('gr. maraino ‚rub, wipe, consume, weaken‘, Pass. ‚verzehre myself, verschwinde allmaehlich‘, marasmos ‚Hinschwinden‘') and Watkins gives it as mer-2, I.2 (whence MARASMUS, AMARANTH). marmaros/marmaron 'block of stone, marble' is the contested item. The traditional etymology, which Nourai follows through Pokorny 736, is: 'marmaros ‚stone, boulder‘ (compare Latin rupes : rumpo), later (after marmairo) ‚white stone, marble‘ (out of it Latin marmor)' - i.e. reduplicated *mer- 'rub, crush', with the 'gleaming' sense a secondary contamination from marmairein 'to sparkle'. Frisk keeps the root but derives it from marnamai 'to fight' (itself Pokorny's mer-5); Beekes (2010) rejects an IE source altogether and calls marmaros Pre-Greek, and Etymonline says simply 'of unknown origin, perhaps originally an adjective meaning ‚sparkling‘'. nodes.derivation: Persian marmar 'marble' is a loanword from Greek marmaros, exactly as drawn. Mo'in says so in as many words in his footnote to the Borhan entry: 'marmar - be-fath-e do mim, az yunani marmaros; arabi va torki ‚marmar‘' (Borhan-e Qate' printed p.1996). The Greek word reached Persian in the Hellenistic/late-antique Near East along with the stone trade and the Byzantine-Sasanian building vocabulary, and it is shared with Aramaic/Syriac marmara, Arabic marmar and Turkish mermer (Wiktionary derives Turkish mermer 'from either Classical Persian marmar or Arabic marmar, both from Ancient Greek marmaros'), so an Aramaic or Arabic relay cannot be excluded for Persian either. The reduplicated shape was kept intact because Persian tolerates the mar-mar pattern; the adjective marmarin is the Persian -in suffix on the loan.

nodes.derivation: Latin marmor, -oris n. 'marble' is real and is the ancestor of the Romance and English words. Whether it was BORROWED from Greek, as the chart's arrow says, is the open question. Pokorny (p.736) and Walde-Pokorny (II 277) say plainly 'out of it Latin marmor' / 'daraus lat. marmor', and Klein agrees ('fr. VL. marmorem, acc. of L. marmor ... fr. Gk. marmaros'). Etymonline is more cautious: 'from Latin marmor, from or cognate with Greek marmaros' - i.e. both may be independent reflexes of a Mediterranean stone-word, which fits Beekes' Pre-Greek analysis of marmaros. Ernout-Meillet treat marmor as one of the neuter material-nouns (LAT.txt l.36618: 'marmor, -oris n.: marbre; et objet de marbre (statue, etc.)'). Given the doubt about the Greek word's own origin, the Greek-to-Latin arrow is likely but not certain, hence plausible.

nodes.derivation: Middle English marbre (mid-12c.), borrowed from Old French, was altered to marbel/marble in the 14th century by dissimilation of the second -r- to -l-, a change Etymonline places in the same period in French itself; marbre survived in English into the early 15th century. The English word thus stands at the end of the chain Greek marmaros (or a Mediterranean word shared with it) > Latin marmor > Old French marbre > English marble, and the derived senses (a sculptured marble, 14c.; the children's glass ball, 1690s) are internal English developments.

nodes.derivation: Both Germanic forms are Watkins' own reconstructions under this root and Nourai reproduces them faithfully. *maron- 'goblin, incubus' gives Old English mare/mere 'incubus', Old Norse mara, Old High German mara, German Mahr, and (with a Slavic branch: Polish zmora, Czech mura) points to a PIE *mora- 'incubus' understood as a derivative of *mer- 'to rub away, harm' - the nightmare being the being that 'presses, crushes' the sleeper. *mur-thra- (suffixed zero-grade *mr-tro-) gives Old English morthor 'murder' beside the shorter *mr-to-m in Old English morth, Old High German mord, Gothic maurthr; Latin mors, mortis is the same *mr-ti- formation. Pokorny p.735 lists 'mr-tro-m in Gothic maurthr, Old English mordor ‚murder‘' in the mer-4 'die' lemma.

nodes.derivation: nightmare is a Middle English compound (c.1300) of night + mare (n.) 'goblin that causes bad dreams, incubus', the latter from Old English mare < Proto-Germanic *maron- of node #17; the sense shifted in the mid-16th century from the incubus itself to the suffocating sensation it causes, and to 'any bad dream' by 1829. murder is Old English morthor (c.1300 murdre, earlier morther) 'secret killing', from Proto-Germanic *murthran, with the -d- spelling reinforced by Anglo-French murdre / Medieval Latin murdrum (itself from the Germanic word). Both are exactly the two English derivatives Watkins lists under mer-2, and Etymonline traces both to 'PIE root *mer- ‚to rub away, harm‘ (also ‚to die‘)'.
